findings.problem: The entry's central measurement is left open to the standard defence, and advocate.best_defense does not raise it. findings.fix: Add two sentences to section two closing the escape on real optics: near-horizon refraction does not magnify, it compresses - the Sun's vertical diameter is flattened by up to about 5 arcmin at the horizon while the horizontal diameter is unchanged, so the measured angle never grows and the required compensation runs the wrong way. findings.problem: "the Solar System - eleven orders of magnitude above the MOND scale" is wrong, and it appears twice. With a0 = 1.2e-10 m/s^2, the Earth's orbital acceleration is GM_sun/r^2 = 5.93e-3 m/s^2, a factor of 4.9e7 = 10^7.7, not 10^11. At Neptune it is 6.5e-6 m/s^2, only 4.7 orders above. Eleven orders is the ratio for the Earth's SURFACE gravity (9.81/1.2e-10 = 8.2e10), which is not what the sentence is about. This sits in the paragraph our own advocate block calls "the only paragraph here that touches the list's actual thesis", so it is the most quotable error in the entry.

findings.problem: Item 365 "Metonic precision." is traced to the 1881 almanac-tabulation paragraph on the ground that "the nineteen-year repeat is the Metonic cycle". It is not — it is the Saros. Rowbotham's own text (sacred-texts za29.htm, p. 153-154, fetched and read) says the repeats occur "in every cycle of between eighteen and nineteen years" and illustrates it with a train passing "every eighteenth day"; the "nineteenth and twentieth years" are table ROWS, i.e. an 18-year interval, and the chapter has already defined that interval as the Saros of 6,585 1/3 days. Dubay's 2018 post frames the same passage as "18 year cycles"; the FES wiki quotes Ball as "eighteen years, or nineteen years... 6585 1/3 days". The Metonic cycle is a lunisolar calendar cycle (235 synodic months to 19 tropical years), which is what the entry's own section five correctly analyses — a different quantity from the one in the source passage. "Metonic", "draconic" and "nineteen" return zero hits in the 1865 Gutenberg text (#69892) and "Metonic" returns zero in the 1881 chapter. This makes three downstream statements overclaims: "Every one of the four quantities the list names... is in this chapter" (which also contradicts gloss paragraph four, where the nineteen-year material is correctly said not to be in the 1865 text), "Rowbotham's chapter supplies every one of the four quantities", and the verdict_challenge's "a search for the four named quantities returned a documented lineage in one chapter". On a page whose product is provenance, this is the load-bearing claim of the whole entry.
findings.fix: Narrow the attribution to what the chapter contains: the node, the Saros and the apogee (the last being a quantity the list does not name). Say that the 1881 recipe recovers the SAROS by counting, not the Metonic cycle, and quote Rowbotham's "every cycle of between eighteen and nineteen years" as the proof. Then note that a Metonic reference does exist in the modern carrier already cited here — the Flat Earth Society wiki quotes T. G. Ferguson (Earth Review, September 1894) quoting Keith: "The cycle of the moon is said to have been discovered by Meton, an Athenian in B.C. 433" — and route item 365 there, or mark it untraced rather than guessed. Delete "Every one of the four quantities the list names... is in this chapter" and "supplies every one of the four quantities and none of the four assertions", replacing both with the count that survives.

findings.problem: "So this material did not reach the modern list through the Victorian proof-list at all: it stayed in Rowbotham's prose chapter for a century and was lifted back out of it directly." The premise is a correctly scoped keyword search ("Saros", "Metonic" and "node" are indeed absent from Carpenter PG #55387 — I re-ran it, zero hits each), but the conclusion is about an ARGUMENT, and the argument is in Carpenter. His numbered proof 66 reads: "It is often said that the predictions of eclipses prove astronomers to be right in their theories. But it is not seen that this proves too much. It is well known that Ptolemy predicted eclipses for six-hundred years, on the basis of a plane Earth, with as much accuracy as they are predicted by modern observers." That is the theory-independence claim this entry identifies as the one descending to Dubay and the FES wiki — including the Ptolemy/600-years detail that Rowbotham takes from Smith and that Dubay reproduces. So the Victorian numbered proof-list carries this material as its own numbered item, and a defender refutes our sentence with one click on a source we cite ourselves. The sentence also carries weight beyond this entry: it is offered as "a small but clean piece of evidence for the project's general finding" about distributors returning to originals.
findings.fix: Replace with what the search actually established: "The technical vocabulary did not travel by this route — the words 'Saros', 'Metonic' and 'node' are not located in the Project Gutenberg text of Carpenter's One Hundred Proofs (1885, ebook #55387). The argument did: Carpenter's proof 66 states the theory-independence claim in his own words, without the cycle names. So the modern list could have had the argument from either, and the four named quantities are the part that can only have come from Rowbotham's chapter." Drop or re-base the "returning to the same few originals" inference, which no longer follows from this case.

What he declines at p. 371 is narrower — that power asymmetries cause the Axis of Evil — and the list does not distinguish the two." Delete "the one item its own authority set down" and "the one item its own authority set aside" wherever they appear.

findings.problem: The TLDR is stronger than the body it summarises — the pattern both prior sweeps flagged, with the quantifier "All six" doing the damage. "All six of these are real features of the microwave sky and Planck says so — its isotropy paper calls their existence 'uncontested'." I read the Planck sentence in context: it is introduced by an enumeration of the lack of large-angle correlation, low variance, hemispherical asymmetry / dipolar modulation, odd-parity preference, and the large southern temperature decrement. That is four of E02's six items. It does not cover item 331 ("ISW correlations ecliptic-linked") — the body's own ISW paragraph says the literature runs the other way on the ecliptic clause — and it does not cover item 336 ("Cosmic isotropy violations"), which the body answers with "Unknown, and reasonable people are on both sides". Planck's very next clause is that the extent to which these features "provide evidence for a violation of isotropy in the CMB remains unclear", so the TLDR has Planck endorsing the reality of the one item Planck explicitly declines to endorse.
findings.fix: Narrow the quantifier to what the body supports: "Four of these six are real features of the microwave sky and Planck says so — its isotropy paper calls their existence 'uncontested'. The other two are the list's own summary label and a claim about the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect that the ISW literature does not support. What the six do not do is agree with each other." Keep the rest of the TLDR unchanged; the figure-coordinates sentence and the scalar sentence are both correct.

findings.problem: The source's conclusion is characterised as "hedged and disjunctive" by quoting up to the disjunction and stopping there, which is the move the hedge rule exists to forbid — performed on the source instead of by the list. The entry quotes: the CMB's characteristics "suggest that our local system … is either a central source or the central depository or 'sink' for the CMB radiation", and concludes that item 336 "states as established what the source states as a suggestion between disjuncts" (`scope_widened`). The next two sentences on the same page read: "This means that the Earth and its neighbors are in the center of the phenomenon." and, four sentences later, "In either model there can be no other conclusion than the orientation of the CMB is purely geocentric." The disjunction is over the mechanism (source or sink), not over the conclusion, which is stated flatly. The immediately preceding sentence is equally flat: "which combination forms an X and Y axes with Earth directly in the center of it all."
findings.fix: Extend the quoted span through "This means that the Earth and its neighbors are in the center of the phenomenon" and "there can be no other conclusion than the orientation of the CMB is purely geocentric", and drop `scope_widened` for 336 — on this passage the list is not stronger than the source, the source is stronger than the list. If a drift finding is still wanted for 336, it has to rest on something else (e.g. that "cosmic isotropy violations" imports the anomaly literature's technical term for a claim the source makes about a place rather than a field), and that is a `category_shifted` argument, not a hedge-dropping one.

findings.field: passage.gloss (finding 1) / refutation opening / steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim / tldr / verdict_challenge.reasoning
findings.problem: The entry's organising claim is that spherical shells and a preferred axis are mutually exclusive evidence — "A sphere centred on you has no axis. An axis has no centre... at most one of these items can be evidence for a central Earth", and in the verdict "the model these items are marshalled for — a central Earth in a spherically symmetric cosmos — predicts no preferred direction at all". The source does not hold a spherically symmetric cosmos. Sungenis's geocentrism is a universe that rotates about a central Earth once a day; that model has a centre AND an axis, and the celestial pole is that axis. Worse, the "[sun-earth]" interpolation Sungenis adds to the quoted sentence shows exactly how he reads the ecliptic result: cosmic structure keyed to our own orbital plane is, for him, further evidence that the Earth is special, not a competing geometry. Shells give centrality, an Earth-keyed axis gives specialness, and the two are consistent as evidence for one conclusion. The advocate block even raises this ("It is a rotation about an axis. An axis is what we claimed") and the preemptive answers a different objection instead — that an unexplained direction is not a claimed centre — leaving the actual hit unanswered. Hutsemekers 2005 itself mentions rotating cosmologies in this connection (astro-ph/0507274, discussion of the mirror-like symmetry: a global rotation "would also induce a rotation of the polarization angles as a function of the distance to the source").
findings.fix: Drop the claim that the two items cannot both be evidence for one conclusion, and keep the weaker, true claim: they are different geometries requiring different physics, and the source welds them with an "in other words" that does no argumentative work. Then answer the axis on its merits, which the entry already does well in IV(a)-(d): the axis does not point at the Earth, it rotates with distance, and its natural frame is the Local Supercluster's, not the Earth's. Recommended replacement for the gloss sentence: "A geocentric cosmos that turns once a day has both a centre and an axis, so these are not formally incompatible; what they are is two unrelated results, resting on different data and different physics, joined by the words 'in other words'." The verdict paragraph's clause "predicts no preferred direction at all" must go with it.

findings.field: passage.gloss (finding 2) / refutation section V / compression.note (third paragraph) / straw_man.detail
findings.problem: The entry's self-declared hardest finding — that Sungenis's ellipsis deletes the CMB so that "the sentence acquires whatever subject the surrounding paragraph supplies — which, on p. 414 of Galileo Was Wrong, is quasars", and that "the claim changes subject from the microwave background to quasars inside a pair of quotation marks" — is materially undercut by the source text. In the Internet Archive OCR of the seventh-edition three-volume scan, the sentence introducing the block quote on printed p. 413 reads: "Lastly, a team studying the orientation of quasars has discovered that they have a preferred axis, the same as they found for radio wavelengths and micro wavelengths (i.e., the CMB)." The book names the microwave background, and glosses "micro wavelengths" as the CMB, one sentence before the quotation. Independently, Urban & Zhitnitsky's own section II.A (arXiv:1011.2425v2, p. 2) says the quasar polarization vectors "tend to identify an axis in the sky which closely align with the direction of the cosmological dipole", and their II.C says the CMB multipole normals point along "the cosmological dipole once again" and the ecliptic — so a single common axis spanning optical, radio and micro is the paper's actual thesis, not something Sungenis manufactured. The mechanical claim is true (the elision does remove the subject of "point", and Sungenis interpolates "[sun-earth]"), but the accusation built on it — that the source is "made to say something about quasars that they said about the microwave background" — is not defensible as written, and it is the first thing a well-informed defender will check. Note also that the entry's IV(d) rebuts an equatorial-frame axis while item 117 claims an ecliptic one; no ecliptic-frame test is reported either way.
findings.fix: Rewrite the finding to what survives: the elision removes the subject of the verb and the interpolation "[sun-earth]" glosses the ecliptic as an Earth-Sun structure, so the compressed item 117 reads as a fact about quasars — but the book itself signposts the CMB one sentence earlier and the cited paper does claim a common axis. Then answer that claim rather than the quotation: the CMB quadrupole/octopole alignment is real and argued at ARG-E01; the quasar A1-A3 axis is near the CMB dipole (astro-ph/0507274 gives the dipole at l=264, b=48 and the quasar axis at l=267, b=69), the 2005 authors call the axis "definitely affected by observational biases", and Urban & Zhitnitsky's own footnote 2 calls the dipole coincidence "mere coincidence" for the purposes of their discussion. Add the strongest form of item 117 to steelman.description and to advocate.best_defense, where it is currently missing.

findings.problem: IV(b) says the handedness flip means "a mirror symmetry about the Galactic plane is a fact about where we sit in the Milky Way... A mechanism tied to the Galaxy, or to the local matter distribution, can produce exactly this". The abstract of the paper cited for the fact says the reverse: "These characteristics make the alignment effect difficult to explain in terms of local mechanisms, namely a contamination by interstellar polarization in our Galaxy" (astro-ph/0507274). The same paper also declines to state the flip as flatly as the entry and the TLDR do: "a counter-clockwise rotation in both the South and North Galactic Caps (S2 symmetry) cannot be totally excluded", "both the slope and the constant of the linear fit depend on the coordinate system", "due to the 180 degree uncertainty, several other complicated or asymmetric solutions to the theta-z relation could be imagined", and the paper explains that a step-like discontinuity at z=0 is expected in general from the way position angles are defined for a structure crossing the observer. The paper's own reading of the mirror symmetry is that it "would be accounted for by a rotation axis close to the A1-A3 axis" — a global rotation, which is nearer the defender's model than ours. advocate.preemptive (b) calls this line "the defender's cleverest move" and instructs that the answer "must not be cut", so the error is pinned in place. It is also load-bearing in the TLDR ("reverses handedness between the galactic hemispheres"), which is where readers meet it first.
findings.fix: Delete "A mechanism tied to the Galaxy, or to the local matter distribution, can produce exactly this; a centre cannot." Replace the paragraph with the hedged version the source supports: the S1 mirror symmetry is the best-defined fit but the paper records that S2 (same handedness in both caps) cannot be totally excluded and that the S1 result depends on the coordinate system through the z=0 discontinuity. Then rest IV on the features that are not coordinate-dependent — the different preferred directions at z~0.5 and z~1.5, the ~30 deg/Gpc rotation, the ~1.5 Gpc alternance, and the observational-bias passage. Soften the TLDR clause to "whose preferred direction rotates about 30 degrees per gigaparsec" and drop the handedness clause, since it cannot carry TLDR weight.

findings.problem: The TLDR asserts that "every independent re-analysis since 2008 ... finds the sky consistent with isotropy." Refutation section seven says the opposite in its own words: "One research programme continues to report the asymmetry. Lior Shamir has published it from SDSS, Pan-STARRS, DES, HST, HSC and JWST deep fields, in refereed venues through 2024-25 ... That exchange is unresolved and this page is not adjudicating it." Shamir's 2024 reply (arXiv:2404.13864, verified) is in part a re-analysis of the same public catalogues, and PASA 41:e038 is refereed. This is recurring failure 2/6 verbatim - the TLDR is stronger than the body it summarises, and the universal quantifier is the load-bearing word. It also breaks the restraint rule the entry's own docstring invokes at point 6 ("E01's restraint rule applies: represent the open part as open"). Highest reader impact of anything here, because the TLDR is what a skimmer takes away.
findings.fix: Replace "every independent re-analysis since 2008 ... finds the sky consistent with isotropy" with a scoped version plus the concession, e.g. "and every re-analysis of Longo's and Shamir's own catalogues by other groups - Galaxy Zoo 2008, Hayes 2017, Iye 2021, Patel & Desmond 2024 - has come back consistent with isotropy, though the group that reports the asymmetry is still publishing and that exchange is open." Keep the 4.0-to-0.29 sigma clause; it is accurate.

findings.problem: Both fields set "the preprint's 'signal exceeding 5 sigma'" against "the peer-reviewed version's axis-free number ... 7.9 x 10^-4, about 3.2 sigma", and the compression note files this under the heading "Link one, Longo to the book: qualifiers removed at the sentence level" as drift evidence. The refereed paper carries the 5 sigma figure too. PLB 699:224 states in its own section 3: "Overall the asymmetry is -0.0607 +/- 0.0118, a 5.15 sigma effect with a probability of 2.5x10^-7 for occurring by chance", and its Table I prints the same numbers (verified in the arXiv:1104.2815 full text, which is the published version). The book therefore quoted a figure that survives intact into the journal article - it dropped no qualifier here, and charging it with one is unfair to the source in a block whose entire purpose is fairness to the source. Each clause is literally true, which is what makes it worse: a defender opens the paper we cite, finds 5.15 sigma on page 8, and concludes we implied a walk-back that never happened. Related arithmetic error in refutation section seven's verdict paragraph: "the significance halves when the axis is not assumed" - 5.15 to 3.16 is a 39% reduction, and in probability it is a factor of 3,000.
findings.fix: Recast as the within-paper contrast, which is real and survives inspection: in PLB 699:224 the sector analysis over pre-chosen right-ascension ranges (165-225 deg and 15 +/- 30 deg, carried over from the earlier study) gives 5.15 sigma, while the unbinned dipole fit that "made no prior assumptions for the dipole axis", after the look-elsewhere penalty computed over 100 randomly chosen axes, gives 7.9 x 10^-4, about 3.2 sigma - and the same axis-free fit in the 2009 preprint, before that penalty, gave 1.51 x 10^-4. Drop the 5 sigma line from the list of hedge-drop evidence entirely; the truncated 1.6 sigma quotation carries the drift finding on its own and is fully verified. Replace "the significance halves" with "the significance drops from 5.15 sigma to about 3.2 sigma".

findings.problem: "The book cites the 2009 preprint and dates it 2009 while printing the 2007 title and a bare DOI stub; the reader who follows the citation lands on a different version of the paper from the one the title names." This does not describe either of the book's actual citations. arXiv:0707.3793 and arXiv:0904.2529 carry the identical title "Evidence for a Preferred Handedness of Spiral Galaxies" (verified on both abs pages; the entry's own sources block assigns that same title to both), so "the 2007 title" identifies nothing and cannot name a different version. What the scan actually shows is two different and better defects. The footnote on Vol. I p. 384 (leaf 397) gives the URL "http://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/0707/0707.3793.pdf, p. 9" and then quotes the abstract of the 2009 paper ("The new study uses 15,158 with redshifts <0.085 ... a signal exceeding 5 sigma"), before adding "In a slightly different version of the same article" with the 0904.2529 URL. The footnote at pp. 240 and 448 (leaves 253, 461) reads: "'Evidence for a Preferred Handedness of Spiral Galaxies,' Michael Longo, Physics Letters B 10.1016, 2009; http://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/0904/0904.2529.pdf" - a preprint title and a truncated DOI attached to a Physics Letters B article that is titled "Detection of a Dipole in the Handedness of Spiral Galaxies with Redshifts z ~ 0.04" and appeared in 2011. On a provenance project this is the wrong sentence to get wrong, and the true version is the stronger one.
findings.fix: Replace with what the scan shows: "The book's citations do not resolve to one document. The footnote at p. 384 quotes the 2009 preprint's abstract under a URL for the 2007 preprint, then flags the next quotation as coming from 'a slightly different version of the same article'. The footnote at pp. 240 and 448 attaches the preprint's title, a truncated DOI ('Physics Letters B 10.1016') and the year 2009 to a journal article that appeared in Physics Letters B in 2011 under a different title. A reader following either citation lands on a preprint, not on the paper named."

findings.field: tldr (and refutation section 5 heading, steelman KERNEL)
findings.problem: The TLDR asserts a uniqueness that the current literature falsifies: "The one genuinely Earth-facing fact is that Andromeda's plane is seen edge-on from here", echoed by section 5's "The one fact that does involve us". Kanehisa, Pawlowski & Libeskind, "Andromeda's asymmetric satellite system as a challenge to cold dark matter cosmology", Nature Astronomy, published 11 April 2025, report a second and stronger Milky-Way-referenced fact: "All but one of Andromeda's 37 satellite galaxies are contained within 107 degrees of our Galaxy", a 4.7-sigma departure from isotropy found in "less than 0.3% (0.5% when accounting for possible observational incompleteness) of Andromeda-like systems", and described in the abstract as "aligned towards the Milky Way". It is by the same Pawlowski group whose 2013 "fortunate" line the entry leans on, it postdates every source cited except the two 2026 preprints, and section 5's selection-effect answer does not touch it — the asymmetry is azimuthal about the MW direction, not an orientation-detectability effect, and the authors explicitly tested observational incompleteness. This is the strongest form of the argument as of 2026 and the steelman does not reach it, so the KERNEL tier is not actually met. The substantive answer is straightforward and strengthens the entry: it is an alignment toward a galaxy 780 kpc away, unchanged if the Sun sat anywhere in the disc, and it is a claim about M31's satellite distribution rather than about the Earth.
findings.fix: Drop the uniqueness in both places — TLDR to "The Earth-facing facts on offer are that Andromeda's plane is seen edge-on from here and that its satellites are lopsided towards our Galaxy", section 5 heading to "The facts that do involve our line of sight, stated at full strength and then answered." Add Kanehisa/Pawlowski/Libeskind 2025 to the KERNEL and to section 5 with the 107-degree, 4.7-sigma and <0.3% figures, and answer it on the same ground section 4 already occupies: the referent is M31 and the MW, two galaxies, and the configuration is invariant under moving the Sun anywhere in the Galactic disc. Add the source: Nature Astronomy (2025), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-025-02480-3.

findings.field: untraceable (paragraph 2, "The geocentric compendium ... was searched in full")
findings.problem: The published search log states: "'Kroupa', 'Ibata', 'M31', 'Tully', 'plane of satellites' and 'disk of satellites' each return zero hits in that text." Tully does not return zero. I re-downloaded the identical artifact — the same Internet Archive item, 5,499,250 bytes and 134,983 lines, matching the fingerprint the entry itself publishes — and "Tully" returns 2 case-insensitive hits. One is substantive: "Next, galaxies in the Fisher-Tully catalogue that showed large amounts of rotation and interval motion (the opposite extreme from the dwarf irregulars) were studied", which sits inside the very redshift-quantization passage the entry assigns to ARG-E12 in the next sentence. The other is OCR noise in a scanned magazine page. The conclusion is unaffected — the Fisher-Tully catalogue is not the satellite-plane literature — but this is the one paragraph written to be checked by a reader with a grep, and it fails on the first try. Kroupa (0), Ibata (0), M31 (0), "plane of satellites" (0) and "disk of satellites" (0) all confirmed correct.
findings.fix: Move Tully out of the zero-hit list and into the E12 sentence: "'Kroupa', 'Ibata', 'M31', 'plane of satellites' and 'disk of satellites' each return zero hits in that text. 'Tully' returns two, one of them OCR noise and the other the Fisher-Tully catalogue inside the redshift-quantization passage that belongs to ARG-E12." This costs nothing and makes the paragraph survive the check it invites.

findings.field: clusters.py E06 note (renders via render.py:180 as the summary line under the verdict chip)
findings.problem: The cluster record reads "A real LambdaCDM tension that has substantially deflated; with Gaia proper motions the Milky Way plane looks transient rather than rotation-supported." render.py line 180 emits a["basis"] — which build.py sets from the cluster note — as the ks-tldr paragraph immediately under the verdict chip, so it is read before anything is expanded. The treatment's section 1 argues the direct opposite at length and with citations: Seo et al. 2024 still get 0.00-3.40%, the Cen A follow-up is titled "remains a challenge", and Sawala's own 2026 follow-up reconciles rather than closes. The published page therefore tells a skim reader the tension has deflated and tells an expanding reader it has not. The agent recorded this in the docstring and correctly kept it out of the prose (no future-tense self-criticism, which is right), but recording is not applying — this is the "recorded, NOT ACTUALLY APPLIED" pattern curmudgeon.md names as the highest-leverage item on the list, now on its fifth occurrence.
findings.fix: Edit clusters.py anchored on the "E06" key, never on the originator= line: replace the note with "A real and still-unresolved LambdaCDM tension. Sawala et al. 2023 answered the Milky Way case and said so; Seo et al. 2024 rebuilt the rarity test and still get 0.00-3.40%, and the Centaurus A result of 2021 is titled 'remains a challenge'. No geocentric content either way." Then re-run tests/run.sh, since the basis string renders into the page.

findings.problem: The block says the book "attributes to the analysts a claim about the CMB rest frame removing the Pioneer effect, which reads as a paraphrase of a position not located in the two JPL review papers the chapter otherwise follows closely (Nieto & Turyshev, CQG 21:4005; Anderson et al., Phys. Rev. D 65:082004)." It IS located in Anderson et al. 2002. Sec. XI of gr-qc/0104064 reports Rosales and Sanchez-Gomez's proposal that "the Pioneer effect represents a new cosmological Foucault experiment", that "the Pioneers are mimicking the role that the rotating Earth plays in Foucault's experiment", and that "a coordinate transformation to the co-moving cosmological coordinate frame would entirely remove the Pioneer effect." The book's Claim #5 (printed p. 408) is a close and substantially faithful paraphrase of that paragraph. The absence claim is correctly scoped and factually false, and it accuses the source of inventing a position it in fact reported accurately.
findings.fix: Replace the last sentence of straw_man.detail with the accurate and sharper version: the book's Claim #5 tracks Anderson et al. 2002 Sec. XI (Rosales and Sanchez-Gomez) closely, but substitutes "Cosmic Microwave Background rest frame" for the paper's "co-moving cosmological coordinate frame" — two different frames, and the substitution is the book's, not the paper's. That is a real, small misrendering and it is checkable; the current sentence is not.

findings.field: refutation (section 5, 'The force the geocentric reading needs cannot exist')
findings.problem: The sentence "Anderson et al. noted in 2002 that the acceleration “is too large to have escaped detection in planetary orbits, particularly for Earth and Mars.”" puts quotation marks around wording that is not Anderson's. Anderson et al. 2002 reads: "The anomalous acceleration is too large to have gone undetected in planetary orbits, particularly for Earth and Mars." The phrase "escaped detection" is Sungenis & Bennett's, from numbered detail 2 at printed p. 401 of the Vol. II OCR: "Large, bound astronomical bodies show no signs of the anomaly, although the acceleration is too large to have escaped detection in planetary orbits, particularly for Earth and Mars." The reviewed book's paraphrase is being published as the reviewed paper's words, on a page whose subject is exactly that failure mode.
findings.fix: Quote Anderson as "too large to have gone undetected in planetary orbits, particularly for Earth and Mars". Then use the book's detail 2 in its own right as a second, stronger concession alongside detail 15 — the source states the planetary-orbit objection itself, in its own numbered list, which is a better find than the one currently claimed.

findings.problem: "The Pioneer anomaly really did point at the Earth — and that is how it was solved" is stronger than every source cited and stronger than the body, which quotes Turyshev et al. 2011 saying "although the direction of the acceleration remains imprecisely determined, we find no support in favor of a Sun-pointing direction over the Earth-pointing or along the spin-axis directions". Turyshev et al. 2012 puts it as "the direction of the anomalous acceleration cannot be determined unambiguously" while "the Doppler residuals improve if one considers a temporally varying acceleration in the direction of the Earth", and calls that merely "suggestive". The 2011 paper adds that "the spin and Earth-spacecraft axes are effectively degenerate". The second clause is also wrong historically: the case was closed by a finite-element thermal model cross-checked against an independent Doppler fit, not by the direction determination. The same overstatement recurs in the refutation ("The direction really did resolve towards the Earth") one clause before the quote that contradicts it, and in the steelman ("the best-fit direction really is Earth-pointing").
findings.fix: TLDR: "The Pioneer anomaly's direction was never pinned down — but the Doppler residuals improve if it points at the Earth, and that is a prediction of the answer, not a problem for it." Then keep the thermal sentence. In the refutation, replace "really did resolve towards the Earth" with the 2012 paper's own formulation (residuals improve for an Earth-directed, temporally varying acceleration; the spin and Earth-spacecraft axes are effectively degenerate), which concedes what the defender is owed without asserting what the papers decline to assert.

findings.field: refutation (section 3, 'The formula has since failed a prediction, in public')
findings.problem: The section loads weight on "four encounters consistent with zero from August 2005 onward, and a description that fits the first group and mispredicts the second", and the advocate.preemptive doubles down ("the load then rests ... on the four post-2007 nulls"). Only one of the four is a genuine misprediction. The entry itself quotes Anderson & Nieto's caveat that the relation models the anomaly "at least for flybys at an altitude of 2000 km or less"; Rosetta II's perigee altitude was 5,322 km and Rosetta III's 2,483 km, both outside that domain, so "where the relation expects a signal" is contestable on the entry's own quoted authority. MESSENGER (2,336 km) is predicted near-zero by the formula, which the entry says two sentences earlier — so counting it among encounters the description "mispredicts" contradicts the same paragraph. Juno (561 km) is the only clean out-of-sample failure, and the section already says so.
findings.fix: Rewrite the closing sentence to: three unexplained encounters 1990-2005; then MESSENGER, which the formula itself predicts near-zero; then Rosetta II and III, both above the 2,000 km altitude at which its authors scoped it; then Juno, at 561 km, inside the domain, predicted ~6 mm/s and measured 0 +/- 0.8. One clean failure, correctly identified, is a better argument than four nulls that a defender can dismantle in a sentence.

findings.field: refutation, chronology of the Juno prediction
findings.problem: "Iorio published the prediction beforehand" is false. Juno's Earth flyby was 9 October 2013; Iorio's paper is arXiv:1311.4218, submitted November 2013, and its own abstract reads "It predicts an anomaly of the order of 6 mm s^-1 for the recent flyby of Juno, occurred on 9 October 2013" — past tense. The prediction was published after the encounter and before the reconstruction (Thompson et al. 2014), which is still a real out-of-sample test but not a pre-registered one. The word "beforehand" is doing rhetorical work a defender will strip out.
findings.fix: "Iorio computed what the Anderson relation demanded — roughly 6 mm/s — and showed that nothing in classical or relativistic gravitation could produce it, before the flyby had been reconstructed. Thompson and colleagues at JPL then reconstructed it and found 0 +/- 0.8 mm/s."

findings.problem: The TLDR's punchline is "the astronomer behind the 2025 headlines says 'our galaxy', not 'the Earth'", and compression.note lists "The referent moves" as one of three things the list changed in transit. Banik's quoted words are indeed "our galaxy" — but the single source we cite for that quote is the University of Portsmouth / RAS National Astronomy Meeting release, whose headline reads "Is Earth inside a huge void? 'Sound of the Big Bang' hints at possible solution to Hubble tension" and whose body says verbatim: "For the idea to stand up, Earth and our solar system would need to be near the centre of a void about a billion light-years in radius and with a density about 20 per cent below the average for the universe as a whole." The Earth-referent is already there, in the professional communication of the result, before any proof list touched it — and it is visible in the URL slug sitting in our own `sources` array (is-earth-inside-a-huge-void-...). A defender who clicks the one link we give for this argument lands on a page that appears to refute our headline sentence in its title.
findings.fix: Do not drop the point — extend it, because the extension is the project's own thesis. Keep "Banik says 'our galaxy'" but state where the substitution actually happens: the referent moves in the press release, not on the list, and the list inherited it. Suggested TLDR clause: "...the astronomer behind the 2025 headlines says 'our galaxy'; his own university's press release had already turned that into 'Earth and our solar system', and the list inherited the swap rather than inventing it." In compression.note, rename the second drift from "The referent moves" to something like "The referent had already moved", and cite the release's own sentence — a drift that begins in science communication and is then hardened by a proof list is a stronger finding for this project than one the list manufactured alone, and it removes the entry's most clickable vulnerability.

findings.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim and refutation §7 (the 15 Mpc centring tolerance)
findings.problem: The entry's decisive quantitative move — the docstring calls it "THE DECISIVE NUMBER" — is Alnes & Amarzguioui's ~15 Mpc centring bound. The quote is verbatim and correctly attributed. But their §V states the scale of the model it was computed for: "When compared to the size of the underdensity, which according to Fig. 2 is around 1500 Mpc...". That is a dark-energy-replacing LTB bubble roughly five times the extent of the ~300 Mpc KBC void the section is discussing, and §7 imports the number straight across ("out to something like 300 Mpc ... How near is set by the microwave dipole: Alnes & Amarzguioui found for their model that the observer must lie within about 15 Mpc"). The scoping phrase "for their model" is present, but the conclusion drawn from it is not scoped: "The centring constraint is a ball roughly 3.6e16 Earth diameters wide", "a hypothesis whose finest available 'here' is a ball 49 million light-years wide". Worse, advocate.best_defense raises exactly this attack ("Your fifteen-megaparsec figure comes from one 2006 paper about one void profile — hardly a law of nature") and advocate.preemptive answers it by restating the same number ("a hypothesis with a 49-million-light-year resolution cannot express the proposition 'the Earth rather than the Sun'"), which is circular. No centring constraint specific to the KBC/Banik void is cited anywhere in the entry.
findings.fix: Add the insensitivity argument, which is the real answer and costs one sentence: the conclusion does not depend on the number. Something like: "That bound is computed for Alnes & Amarzguioui's own model, a ~1500 Mpc underdensity built to replace dark energy, and no equivalent bound has been published for the shallower ~300 Mpc void at issue here. It does not matter which way that number moves. The Earth-Sun distance is 5e-12 Mpc; the tolerance would have to tighten by more than fifteen orders of magnitude before the hypothesis could express the sentence 'the Earth rather than the Sun'." Then rewrite the preemptive to point at the insensitivity rather than at the 49-million-light-year figure.

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py, cluster E09 `note` (renders as the basis line under the verdict chip, scripts/render.py line 180)
findings.problem: The cluster note reads: "The local-void reading was tested directly on 1295 supernovae and excluded at 4-5σ." Kenworthy, Scolnic & Riess exclude, at 4-5σ, sharp-edged LTB underdensities with |delta| > 20% (5σ bound delta < 27% on scales above 69 h^-1 Mpc) — verified against their abstract. They do not exclude "the local-void reading", which is being argued in MNRAS as of 2025 by Banik & Kalaitzidis and which this treatment's §5 concedes at full strength. The basis line therefore states flatly the one thing §5, §6 and the TLDR go out of their way not to say, and it renders in the summary line next to the verdict chip, where skim readers who never expand the entry will meet it. The treatment's docstring note 3 diagnoses this correctly and, correctly per the house rule, did not edit clusters.py or comment on our record in the published prose — so this survives as an integrator action, and it is the E01/E03 "reported, NOT ACTUALLY APPLIED" pattern recurring.
findings.fix: Integrator: edit scripts/clusters.py anchored on the cluster key "E09", never on a positional line. Replace the note with something the body supports, e.g.: "Two rival explanations of one number, counted as two proofs. Kenworthy et al. 2019 exclude sharp-edged voids deeper than 20% at 4-5σ on 1295 supernovae; a shallower local void is still argued in MNRAS. Either way the region is tens to hundreds of megaparsecs across and does not single out the Earth." Also record the change in review/corrections.json — the old line is a published overstatement, not merely a stale one.

findings.problem: The published block asserts that "'Interplanetary' returns 22 hits in (B), every one of them either a Maxwell quotation about the aether or a discussion of JPL's probe-navigation equations", and the docstring adds "None about dust." I downloaded the same OCR file (item galileo-was-wrong-the-church-was-right-sungenis-vol-1-3-complete, 5,499,250 bytes) and enumerated all 22. The count is exactly right; the characterisation is not. Several hits are neither category - the 1961 Venus radar contact and the Shapiro/Wallace speed-of-light dispute (4 hits), Galileo's comets in The Assayer, the Mercury perihelion residual, and a general remark about space probes reaching their destinations. One hit is squarely about interplanetary dust: 'a gravitational frequency shift of pioneer signals proportional to distance and the density of the interplanetary dust cannot be responsible for the anomaly; known properties of the dust are not large enough to produce the observed acceleration.' The 'no_source' conclusion is unaffected - nothing in the text argues from zodiacal or Kuiper structure - but this is the one sentence in the entry that a defender can falsify in five minutes with a public download, and it sits in the block whose whole function is to prove the search was rigorous.
findings.fix: Replace the characterisation with what the census supports: 'Interplanetary' returns 22 hits in (B): Maxwell quotations about the aether, the JPL probe-navigation and 1961 Venus-radar material on the speed of light, and single mentions of comets, the Mercury perihelion residual and the Pioneer anomaly - where interplanetary dust is raised and dismissed as a cause of the anomaly. None is an argument from zodiacal-cloud or Kuiper-belt structure. Drop 'None about dust' from the docstring.

findings.problem: Misattributed quotation. The text reads: each component 'is allowed to have a plane of symmetry that is different from the Ecliptic' (San et al., A&A 666:A107, 2022). That sentence is not in the 2022 ZodiPy paper; it is in Cosmoglobe DR2 III, arXiv:2408.11004 (2024), which this entry already cites two lines earlier. The 2022 paper's wording is 'each component is allowed to have some inclination i and ascending node Omega, with respect to the ecliptic.' The neighbouring San-attributed claim is fine - 'All IPD components, except the Earth-trailing feature, are distributed symmetrically around the Sun with respect to the ecliptic plane' is verbatim in the 2022 paper - which makes the error easy to miss and easy to fix.
findings.fix: Re-point the quotation to Cosmoglobe DR2 III (arXiv:2408.11004, 2024), or quote the 2022 paper's own wording instead.

findings.problem: "To make the comb appear you must first place the observer on a body moving at all three of those speeds and take them out" is false for the periodicity the entry leads with, and it contradicts the sentence two lines above it. Napier & Guthrie's 37.5 km/s comb is galactocentric: two subtractions. Humphreys' own text (p. 96) says the galactocentric redshift compensates "for the Earth's motion around the Sun and the Sun's motion around our galaxy's centre"; the 556 km/s CMB step is a further transformation used in Tifft's CBR-rest-frame papers, which is what the entry's own preceding sentence ("Tifft's own later refinement went further in the same direction") already says. Bajan et al. say "galactocentric radial velocities OR using CMB reference frame" — either two or three, not all three. The TLDR gets this right ("galactocentric or microwave-background"); the body overstates it. Worse, this exact point is the source's own printed rebuttal, unanswered here: Bennett, Vol. II ch. 10, printed p. 298 of the same three-volume scan the entry quotes — "subtraction or correction is only done for the first two motions - the orbit around the sun and the solar motion around the galaxy center, the galactocentric frame of reference! The Milky Way motion and the motion towards Leo were unknown at the time and were not taken into account, yet they represent the largest component of the Earth's motion - about 600 km/s! ... Unless, of course, the motions of the Earth are fictitious!" Neither the refutation nor advocate.best_defense engages it, so the strongest form of the source's answer to our load-bearing section goes unmet.
findings.fix: Replace "all three of those speeds" with "the first two of those speeds", and add a short paragraph to section II answering Bennett: the answer is in the book's own footnote on printed p. 417, which lists Tifft's CBR-rest-frame papers (Astrophysics and Space Science 239:35, 1996; J. Astrophys. Astr. 18:415, 1997), i.e. the periodicity is also reported after the full ~600 km/s is removed. So the geocentric reading has to call the corrections fictitious in one frame while spending a result that only exists in another. Add the Vol. II p. 298 passage to advocate.best_defense so the page is seen to have met it.

findings.field: clusters.py E12 (note and real_source) - renders as the published basis line

findings.field: passage.gloss (para 3) and compression.note ("Two: a scope is widened...")
findings.problem: The Sungenis-to-Humphreys link is asserted rather than shown, and the two specifics offered as evidence do not survive checking. In the OCR text this entry uses (Internet Archive item galileo-was-wrong-the-church-was-right-sungenis-vol-1-3-complete, 5,499,250 bytes), the section at printed pp. 417-420 argues from Tifft, a Sky & Telescope item, Matthews in Science and Koo & Kron; none of Humphreys' geometry, arithmetic or one-in-a-trillion figure is located anywhere in that text, and no figure caption crediting Humphreys is located in it either - so "once reproduces a figure from" is unsupported by the entry's own stated provenance route (docstring note 7). "Cites twice by title" is also wrong: the title is located at printed pp. 284, 398, 432 and 580, in the bibliography at p. 631, and in a web-link list at p. 694. So the section does not compress Humphreys' derivation; it argues in parallel with it. This matters because compression.note's second published finding ("a scope is widened by about nine orders of magnitude") is built on the section being downstream of Humphreys.
findings.fix: Keep the finding, drop the chain claim. The part that verifies, and it is enough, is the p. 398 footnote: the book cites Humphreys' TJ paper by title and records that he holds the galaxy, not the Earth, to be the centre, and that "Both Humphreys and Gentry posit that the Earth has diurnal and translational motion" - then heads its own section "Centered Around the Earth" anyway. Rewrite as "the same argument in its strongest published form belongs to someone who rejects the conclusion - and the book cites him by title at pp. 398 and 432 and names him as a galactocentric rival", delete "twice" and delete the figure claim (or supply a page).

findings.problem: The steelman says the solar quadrupole "has since been measured, twice, by methods that do not use Mercury" and then immediately names "ranging to the MESSENGER spacecraft in orbit at Mercury" as the second method - which refutation section 4 itself describes as measuring J2 "from Mercury's own orbit". This is the exact sentence the preemptive designates as the answer to the advocate's circularity objection (rated 3/5), so the load-bearing reply invites the objection it is meant to close. Compounding it, the advocate's charge as drafted is factually wrong about the paper: Park et al. (AJ 153:121, 2017) state they decouple the effects of beta and J2 by taking gamma from the Cassini Shapiro-delay result rather than fitting the PPN parameters and J2 together.
findings.fix: Replace "twice, by methods that do not use Mercury" with "twice, by routes that do not depend on the perihelion residual - one of them without Mercury at all". Then add one sentence to the same paragraph, which is the strongest available answer and is currently absent: Park et al. did not fit J2 against beta and gamma simultaneously - they imported gamma from Cassini and solved for beta and J2 separately, so the degeneracy Dicke identified is broken by data from outside the fit. Correct the advocate's best_defense to charge something the paper actually does, or the preemptive is answering a phantom.

findings.problem: The refutation answers the list's fragment, not the source our own gloss quotes. The gloss locates the argument at Chapter 4 p. 198 (Hoyle: the centre "to be used for any set of bodies depends on the way in which the local system is considered to be isolated from the universe as a whole") and at Chapter 10 p. 598 ("make Earth the immovable barycenter of the universe") - a frame-choice argument about the mass centre of the whole universe, closed with a theological possibility claim ("Certainly no one can object, then, if God had decided long ago to put the Earth in that very barycenter"). Verified verbatim in the OCR. The refutation answers with Sun-Earth versus Sun-Jupiter two-body arithmetic, which is orthogonal to that claim: nothing in the 449 km / 742,900 km comparison bears on where the barycentre of the universe is, and the paragraph never states the conclusion a reader needs (that the solar system's mass centre sits inside or just outside the Sun, 1 AU from the Earth).
findings.fix: Add a paragraph answering the source's version: (a) a barycentre is a coordinate origin, not a dynamically privileged seat - nothing 'rests' there and no observation distinguishes an object at one; (b) what the planetary ephemeris actually fits is relative accelerations, which are unchanged by the choice; (c) the solar-system mass centre is never more than about 2.2 solar radii from the Sun's centre, so on the source's own arithmetic the Earth is not in it; (d) cross-link ARG-R01, where the general-covariance form of Hoyle's point is answered - it is already in `related` but the reader is never routed there. Keep the existing mass-ratio calculation as the answer to item 104's fragment, labelled as such.

findings.field: passage.locator, passage.gloss (p.146/147/149 cites), compression.note (same three), sources[0], and the module docstring
findings.problem: Every citation to the primary source names the wrong chapter, the wrong chapter title and the wrong pages of the archive item it explicitly identifies. In item GallileoWasWrong the quoted material is Chapter 10, 'Mathematical Models of a Geocentric Universe', at printed footers 626-629, confirmed against that item's own table of contents ('Nightingale's Geocentrism 625 / Lynden-Bell's Geocentrism 626 / Barbour and Bertotti's Geocentrism 628') and the running head 'Chapter 10 Galileo Was Wrong'. Phrase-by-phrase: 'general proof that the angular momentum of any closed universe is zero', 'fixed and undisturbed cradle', 'inadvertently vindicated geocentrism' and 'completely exonerate ... if the universe is closed' are all on p. 627 (entry says 146); 'geocentrism has been established ... in 1905', the passage.quote, is on p. 628 (entry says 'the page footer numbered 147'); 'by assuming a non-rotating universe' and the '[e.g., the universe]' / '[e.g., the Earth]' brackets are on p. 629 (entry says 149). Printed pages 145-149 of that item are Chapter 3 (Hawking, Sagan's Pale Blue Dot, gamma-ray bursts) and contain nothing Machian. The strings 'Modern Science & the Acceptance of Geocentrism by Principle', '2013', 'Popov', 'Chapters 1 to 6' and 'Previous five editions' occur zero times in that item's OCR text ('Gallileo was wrong_djvu.txt', 3,335,538 bytes); the title page is the Volume I CD edition, ISBN 0-9779640-0-0. The sources label also gives two impossible overlapping ranges (Ch. 9 pp. 145-149 and Ch. 2 pp. 133-154). Our own A03 entry cites this same item at printed p. ~841, which I confirmed at footer 840-841, Chapter 12 — a 'Chapters 1 to 6' volume does not reach p. 841. The offsets are a uniform +481, which with the Popov material suggests a 2013 seventh-edition volume with per-volume pagination was actually read; if so, works.py puts chapters 7-13 in Vol. II and passage.work='WRK-SUNGENIS-2006' (Vol. I, 2006) is wrong too. As published, a reader following our URL and page number lands on Carl Sagan.
findings.fix: Do not ship until the locator matches a text. If the item named is the text read: 'Chapter 10, "Mathematical Models of a Geocentric Universe", printed pages 626-629 of the Internet Archive OCR text of item GallileoWasWrong (title page: Volume I, The Scientific Evidence, ISBN 0-9779640-0-0)', with gloss and compression.note cites moved 146->627, 147->628, 149->629, and the 'front matter is the seventh edition, Volume 1, 2013' sentence and the 'Chapters 1 to 6 vs Chapter 9' paragraph deleted, since neither string is in that item. If a 2013 seventh-edition volume was in fact read, name that printing, add it to works.py, and change passage.work off WRK-SUNGENIS-2006, because works.py assigns chapters 7-13 to Vol. II. Also withdraw the record_problems entry against clusters.py's year=2006: that record is correct and the defect was ours.

findings.problem: The Mach bucket quotation is not the wording of the edition we cite, and our own sentence asserting it is not out of context is false. We print: 'Try to fix Newton's bucket and rotate the heaven of fixed stars and then prove the absence of centrifugal forces,' framed as Mach challenging the reader, followed by 'That is not a misquotation and it is not out of context.' In the printing our sources name (archive cu31924004010504, McCormack second English edition, Open Court 1902) the sentence is in the Appendix at p. 543 and reads: 'Can we fix Newton's bucket of water, rotate the fixed stars, and then prove the absence of centrifugal forces? The experiment is impossible, the idea is meaningless, for the two cases are not, in sense-perception, distinguishable from each other.' Searches of that full text for 'Try to fix Newton' and 'rotate the heaven' return zero hits, and our sources label points only at pp. 231-232, where the 'several leagues thick' remark is. It is a rhetorical question Mach answers in the next breath, not a dare he leaves open. On a page whose thesis is that quotations lose their qualifiers as they pass through movement compilations, publishing a secondary-literature variant is the single most exploitable line in the file.
findings.fix: Quote as printed and keep the following sentence, which helps us: 'Can we fix Newton's bucket of water, rotate the fixed stars, and then prove the absence of centrifugal forces? The experiment is impossible, the idea is meaningless, for the two cases are not, in sense-perception, distinguishable from each other' (Appendix, p. 543 of the McCormack second English edition). Add the Appendix page to the sources label alongside pp. 231-232, and delete 'That is not a misquotation and it is not out of context'; the accurate version is that the substance is Mach's and the sentence is quoted here as he wrote it.

findings.problem: The strongest defence in the file is rated 4 — 'must be answered in the body' — and is not answered in the body, as preemptive (b) itself says: 'THE ANGULAR-MOMENTUM REPLY NEEDS ONE MORE SENTENCE IN THE BODY.' The advocate block is stripped from the published corpus by build.py and guarded by a test ('advocate mode panel is INTERNAL - never rendered to the page'), so the reply reaches no reader. The objection — that in a relational theory you do not get to compute 'the angular momentum of the universe' in an outside frame and wave it at us — goes directly at the section the entry calls 'the centre of it', and a reader who thinks of it finds nothing.
findings.fix: Land preemptive (b) in the third section: the vanishing is a constraint on the matter itself, not an absolute-space quantity imported from outside, which is why Lynden-Bell, Katz and Bicak present it as a vindication of Mach rather than of Newton, and why Barbour reaches the same restriction from pure invariance under time-dependent rotations with no background at all — two independent relational routes to the same exclusion. Bondi & Samuel supply a third citation for it in a source already in our list: their Mach5 entry reads 'In EC it is claimed that the total angular momentum of a closed universe must vanish' (gr-qc/9607009).

findings.problem: 'a companion note reproduces the 0.76" parallax of Proxima Centauri in the geostatic version' cites nothing a reader can follow, and the number is not in the paper we do cite. Popov's Eur. J. Phys. 34:383 paper (full text of arXiv:1301.6045v2, 20,580 characters extracted and searched) contains no occurrence of 'parallax', 'Proxima' or 'arcsec'. The only companion document is a one-page corrigendum, Eur. J. Phys. 34 (2013) 817, DOI 10.1088/0143-0807/34/3/817 (Crossref gives the page range as 817-817), which is mentioned in the module docstring but appears nowhere in the eleven-item sources list, and which I could not obtain. This is the shape of the batch-8 'the Pacific sea floor' finding: a specific figure in a rendered field with no locatable origin.
findings.fix: Either name it — 'Popov's corrigendum, Eur. J. Phys. 34 (2013) 817' — verify the figure in it, and add it to sources with the DOI; or delete the clause. The KERNEL does not need it: Popov's published Sun-Earth-Mars result plus Assis's bulge, pendulum and Coriolis derivations already carry the concession.

findings.field: refutation (section "Fourth, the measurement, with the numbers")
findings.problem: Two numbers are attributed to Zhang & Stebbins, PRL 107:041301, but they exist only in the superseded arXiv v2, not in the published version the entry cites. We write "(SPT gives < 13 µK²)" and "miss the supernovae by Δχ² > 195". The published paper (arXiv v3, the one served at the abs URL in our own sources list) reads: "The South Pole telescope (SPT) collaboration [18] found ΔT² < 6.5µK² (95% upper limit) and the Atacama cosmology telescope (ACT) collaboration [19] found ΔT² < 8µK²", and "Hubble bubble models consistent with the SPT result have Δχ² > 209 (χ² > 814)". Version v2 does say 13 µK² and Δχ² > 195, so the source of the error is identifiable. The error also inverts the ranking of the two experiments: our parenthetical presents SPT as the looser bound, whereas in the published paper SPT is the tighter one and is the limit the headline "two orders of magnitude" comparison is made against. A defender who opens the cited paper finds this in the first column.
findings.fix: Replace "(SPT gives < 13 µK²)" with "(SPT, the tighter of the two, gives < 6.5 µK²)" and "Δχ² > 195" with "Δχ² > 209". Add "published version, arXiv v3" to the Zhang & Stebbins source label so the next writer does not re-import v2 figures, and correct the same two numbers in the module docstring's note 5.

findings.problem: The closing sentence claims the measurement "excludes by two orders of magnitude the only version of a non-Copernican universe anybody has built." That is an unscoped universal about an entire literature, of exactly the class the house rule bans, in a phrasing the ratchet regex does not match. It is also false on the evidence of the very page of Ellis arXiv:1103.2335 we rely on for the "typical observationally viable model": p. 15 says "Actually you don't need a void to explain the observations; more general models can do the job", and the same section reports Bolejko and Sussman arguing the improbability problem is eased with "a Szekeres rather than LTB solution". Section six carries the same overclaim in miniature ("What is on offer is a Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi void"). A defender only has to quote our own cited source back at us.
findings.fix: Rewrite the clause as scoped to what was tested: "...and excludes by two orders of magnitude the spherically symmetric LTB void models that were built to replace dark energy — the class the kSZ test was aimed at." In section six change "What is on offer is a Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi void" to "What has actually been built and fitted is a Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi void", and add Ellis's own caveat that more general models can do the job.

findings.problem: The refutation states the kSZ result as an unqualified exclusion and never publishes the survival window the cited paper states in the same paragraph as the numbers we do quote: "only models with Ω₀ → 1 or z_edge → 0 (z_edge < ~0.2, corresponding to void radius < 0.6 h⁻¹ Gpc) survive this test". The entry's own research note 5 records this qualification, so it was seen and then left out of the published prose. The omission has a visible consequence: section six's exemplar — Ellis's "typical observationally viable model", an underdense region of 160-250 h⁻¹ Mpc — sits well inside the surviving window, so the page excludes a class in section four and then illustrates the prize with a member of the class that survives, without telling the reader the two are different.
findings.fix: Add one sentence at the end of section four: "The paper is explicit about where the test stops: voids small enough that the underdensity ends below z ≈ 0.2 — radius under about 0.6 h⁻¹ Gpc — survive the kSZ bound, and are excluded instead by failing the supernovae, which is why the two tests are quoted together." Then in section six, mark Ellis's specimen as a member of that smaller class.

findings.field: clusters.py R12 `note` — renders as the summary line of the Refutation section on docs/index.html
findings.problem: The rendered one-line summary of our refutation reads "It is not merely assumed — it is tested. The kSZ power spectrum rules out Gpc-scale off-centre void models." The entry's own docstring note 7 judges this line unsupported by the paper and proposes a replacement, and records it as "Reported in record_problems; clusters.py NOT touched" — but there is no record_problems file in the repository, clusters.py is unchanged, and the line is live in docs/index.html directly under the REFUTED chip. "Off-centre" is also the wrong descriptor: the models at issue put us near the centre, and the off-centre observers are the distant ones whose motion sources the kSZ signal. This is the E01/E03 "recorded, not actually applied" pattern for at least the fifth time, in the most prominent position the cluster record reaches.
findings.fix: Edit clusters.py anchored on the "R12" key (never on the originator= line) so the note reads: "It is not merely assumed — it is tested. The kSZ power spectrum rules out the LTB void models deep enough to mimic dark energy." Rebuild and re-run tests/run.sh.
